solution.concept_anchor: Article 300A — property right after 44th Amendment, stringent test removed

statement_analysis.statement: Prior to the 44th Amendment (1978), property rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 were Fundamental Rights subject to the reasonableness test under Article 19(5).
statement_analysis.reason: Before the 44th Amendment, property was a Fundamental Right and the State's restriction on it had to pass the Article 19(5) reasonable restriction test — making it difficult to legislate socialist redistributive laws.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Amendment, the right to property under Article 300A can only be restricted through legislation, but such legislation is no longer subject to the stringent Article 19(5) reasonable restriction test applicable to Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 300A requires legal authority for deprivation but as a constitutional right (not FR), it is not tested against Article 19(5) — this fundamentally reduced the judicial hurdle for socialist legislation.

statement_analysis.statement: The deletion of property from the list of Fundamental Rights effectively eliminated all tension between property-related legislation and Directive Principles of State Policy.
statement_analysis.reason: While the deletion significantly reduced the tension, it did not eliminate it entirely — Article 300A still provides a constitutional right to property, and other FRs (such as Article 14) can still be invoked against state acquisition actions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may select 'all three' knowing Statements 1 and 2 are correct, and carelessly accepting Statement 3 without noticing that 'effectively eliminated all tension' is a scope-extension overstatement.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Before 44th Amendment, property FRs were subject to 19(5) test — this is accurate. Mark correct.
Statement 2: Post-44th Amendment, Article 300A is a constitutional right not subject to 19(5) stringency — accurate. Mark correct.
Statement 3: 'Eliminated all tension' is an overstatement — Article 300A still provides property protection, and Article 14 can still be used against acquisition. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — correct option is (d) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses 'effectively eliminated all tension' — a classic scope-extension trap. Students who correctly recall that the 44th Amendment greatly reduced the FR-DPSP property conflict may accept 'eliminated all tension' without pausing to note that Article 300A and Article 14 still generate constitutional tension with state acquisition and redistribution laws. The partial truth in Statement 3 is that tension was greatly reduced — not eliminated.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment (1978) fundamentally altered the constitutional landscape by removing property from the Fundamental Rights chapter.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Before 1978, Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 were Fundamental Rights. State restrictions had to satisfy the Article 19(5) reasonableness test — this made land reform and resource redistribution legislation vulnerable to court challenge.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 300A requires deprivation to be authorised by law, but as it is outside Part III, the strict Article 19(5) test does not apply — significantly lowering the threshold for socialist legislation.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Property tension was reduced, not eliminated. Article 300A's 'authority of law' requirement still generates litigation. Article 14 (equality) can still be invoked against arbitrary acquisitions. The tension shifted rather than disappeared.

Value Addition:
• Article 300A is described as a 'constitutional right' (not FR) — an important classification distinction.
• The tension between property rights and socialist DPSPs was the dominant constitutional conflict of the first three decades of the Republic.
• After the 44th Amendment, the main FR-DPSP conflicts shifted to Articles 14 and 19 (freedoms) — Article 31C's protection against these challenges became more significant.

solution.concept_anchor: Three-tier wage hierarchy — minimum, fair, living wage definitions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know 'living wage' is the highest tier and 'minimum wage' is the lowest may correctly place A and C but then confuse 'fair wage' and 'floor wage', mismatching B and D.
elimination_logic: Living wage (Article 43 mandate) is the highest tier — covering full human dignity including social needs. A→3.
Fair wage is above minimum but below living — a middle tier that theoretically enables savings and modest surplus. B→1.
Minimum wage is the lowest tier — covering bare physical subsistence; the Minimum Wages Act 1948 is its statutory expression. C→4.
Floor wage (Code on Wages 2019) is a new national baseline set below or at the minimum wage level across states — the newest and lowest statutory concept. D→2.
Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'floor wage' introduced by the Code on Wages 2019 is a new concept below minimum wage — students who have not updated their knowledge post-2019 may confuse it with minimum wage or living wage. The conflation trap puts 'floor wage' adjacent to 'minimum wage' in the list, testing whether students know that floor wage is actually a sub-minimum national baseline, not synonymous with minimum wage or living wage.
solution.final_explanation:
The wage hierarchy has four distinct levels, and Article 43 occupies the highest aspirational level.

• A (Living wage) — Matches 3 (Full human dignity standard covering social needs beyond subsistence): Article 43 mandates this as the constitutional ideal.
• B (Fair wage) — Matches 1 (Above minimum subsistence, below living wage standard): A middle tier that enables modest surplus; not expressly in the Constitution but recognised in policy.
• C (Minimum wage) — Matches 4 (Bare physical subsistence level; floor under the Minimum Wages Act 1948): The statutory floor before 2019; still the core of wage legislation.
• D (Floor wage) — Matches 2 (New national baseline introduced below or at minimum wage level by Code on Wages 2019): The newest statutory concept, setting a national sub-floor to prevent races to the bottom across states.

Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → Option (b).

Value Addition:
• Unichoyi v. State of Kerala — SC validated minimum wage as a pragmatic intermediate step while acknowledging living wage as the constitutional goal.
• The Code on Wages 2019 consolidates four major labour codes — Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Wages Act, Payment of Bonus Act, and Equal Remuneration Act.
• Article 43 is the only DPSP that explicitly targets a specific wage level (living wage) rather than mere 'adequacy'.

solution.concept_anchor: Property Owners Association 2024 — SC overrules Krishna Iyer view on 39(b)
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students aware that there was a landmark 2024 ruling on Article 39(b) may confuse which position the Court adopted — many associate 39(b) with socialist expansion and assume the Court endorsed the expansive view.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The 2024 nine-judge bench explicitly rejected the expansive view — it held that NOT all private property qualifies as 'material resources of the community'. Option (a) states the opposite of the ruling.

Eliminate (b): The ruling did not exclude all private property from 39(b) — it said the determination depends on the nature, characteristics, and impact of the resource, not that all private property is outside 39(b).

Confirm (c): The Court overruled Justice Krishna Iyer's broad reading from earlier cases (State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy; Sanjeev Coke) and held that the characterisation of private property as 'material resources' requires case-by-case analysis based on resource characteristics.
Eliminate (d): The ruling did not hold that only publicly owned resources qualify — it held that some private resources may qualify depending on their nature, impact, and community significance.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 2024 ruling is counterintuitive for students trained on socialist DPSP jurisprudence, which was broadly expansive under Justice Krishna Iyer's reading. Students expect the nine-judge bench to have reaffirmed the expansive view (all private property = community resources) because that aligns with the socialist ethos. The Court's limiting ruling — restricting the scope of 39(b) — goes against this expectation, making option (a) the most tempting wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 39(b) directs the State to distribute ownership and control of material resources of the community to subserve the common good. The critical interpretive question is whether 'material resources of the community' includes privately owned resources.

• Option (a): Incorrect — The 2024 nine-judge bench rejected the broad reading; it did NOT hold that all private property is covered by 39(b).
• Option (b): Incorrect — The Court did not rule that all private property is excluded; some private resources can qualify depending on their nature and characteristics.
• Option (c): Correct — The bench overruled Justice Krishna Iyer's expansive interpretation (from Ranganatha Reddy and Sanjeev Coke) and held that whether private property constitutes 'material resources of the community' under 39(b) depends on a contextual assessment of the resource's nature, characteristics, and societal impact.
• Option (d): Incorrect — The ruling explicitly left open the possibility that qualifying private resources may fall within 39(b)'s scope.

Value Addition:
• Justice Krishna Iyer's expansive view — that the word 'community' in 39(b) covers all resources within the national territory — had influenced socialist legislation for decades.
• The 2024 ruling shifts the interpretive framework from categorical inclusion to case-by-case contextual analysis.
• Article 31C's protection of 39(b) laws from FR challenge remains unaffected by the 2024 ruling.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 39(a) directing equal and adequate means of livelihood for men and women is an original provision of the Constitution as adopted in 1950.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 39(a) was part of the original DPSP chapter in the Constitution of 1950 — it has not been added by any amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 39(f) on children's healthy development and protection from exploitation was part of the original Constitution of 1950.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 39(f) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 — it is not an original provision.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 41 on the right to work, education, and public assistance is an original provision of the Constitution as adopted in 1950.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 41 was in the original Constitution — it has not been inserted by any subsequent amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 43B on promotion of co-operative societies is an original provision of the Constitution as adopted in 1950.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 43B was inserted by the 97th Constitutional Amendment in 2011 — the most recent addition to the DPSP chapter.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who remember that several DPSPs were added but cannot precisely recall which ones may count three as original, selecting 'Only three'.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 (39(a) original): Part of the original 1950 Constitution — correct.
Statement 2 (39(f) original): Added by 42nd Amendment 1976 — NOT original. Incorrect.
Statement 3 (41 original): Article 41 is original — correct.

Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — correct option is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who loosely recall that 'most DPSPs are original' may count three as correct, selecting option (c). The trap is that Article 39(f) is often mentally grouped with other Article 39 sub-clauses as original — but it was the Emergency-era addition. Similarly, Article 43B's relatively recent addition (2011) may be forgotten. Knowing precisely which socialist DPSPs are non-original (39(f), 43A, 43B, 38(2)) is the key discriminating knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing original DPSP provisions from amendment-inserted additions is a recurring UPSC precision test.

• Statement 1 (39(a)) — Correct: Article 39(a) is an original provision from 1950, directing equal and adequate means of livelihood for men and women.
• Statement 2 (39(f)) — Incorrect: Article 39(f) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — it is not original.
• Statement 3 (41) — Correct: Article 41 on work, education, and public assistance is an original DPSP provision.
• Statement 4 (43B) — Incorrect: Article 43B was inserted by the 97th Amendment (2011) — the most recent DPSP addition.

Only two statements (1 and 3) describe original provisions — correct option is (b).

Value Addition:
• Non-original socialist DPSPs: 39(f) (42nd Amdt), 43A (42nd Amdt), 38(2) (44th Amdt), 43B (97th Amdt).
• The 42nd Amendment (1976) is responsible for the most new DPSP additions in a single amendment.
• Articles 39(b) through 39(e) are all original DPSP provisions — only 39(f) was added later.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 42 vs Article 39(e) — maternity vs unsuitable vocation protection
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are about women workers may assume R (39(e)) explains A (42's maternity mandate), not recognising that 39(e) is about unsuitable vocations — a different legal ground entirely.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion correct? Article 42 does mandate maternity relief as a specific constitutional directive to the State — and this has been used to sustain maternity benefit legislation. Yes, A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason correct? Article 39(e) protects health and strength of men, women, and children from unsuitable economic vocations — it does not specifically address maternity. R as stated claims 39(e) is the constitutional basis for maternity benefit legislation — this is incorrect; that basis is Article 42, not 39(e). R is incorrect.
Step 3: Since R is incorrect, the correct option is (c).
A correct, R incorrect — confirm option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Articles 42 and 39(e) both protect women workers but on entirely different grounds. Article 42 covers maternity relief and humane conditions; Article 39(e) covers protection from economically coerced unsuitable vocations. Reason (R) misattributes the constitutional basis of maternity benefit legislation to Article 39(e) instead of Article 42. Students who recall both provisions protect women will assume R supports A without checking whether 39(e) actually addresses maternity — it does not.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 42 and 39(e) protect different dimensions of women's (and workers') welfare.

Assertion (A): Article 42 constitutionally mandates the provision of maternity relief — correct. This is the specific DPSP basis for the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and its 2017 amendment.

Reason (R): Article 39(e) provides the constitutional basis for maternity benefit legislation — incorrect. Article 39(e) protects health and strength of men, women, and children against unsuitable vocations forced by economic necessity. It does not address maternity. The constitutional basis for maternity benefits is Article 42, not 39(e).

Since A is correct but R is incorrect — correct option is (c).

Value Addition:
• The two-provision test: Article 42 = maternity relief and humane conditions; Article 39(e) = protection against economically forced unsuitable work.
• Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000) read Article 42 with Article 21 — not with 39(e).
• Article 39(e) has legislative expressions in the Factories Act and Mines Act — not in the Maternity Benefit Act.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C shield — laws for 39(b)/39(c) immune from Art 14 and 19 challenge
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Ninth Schedule laws enjoy immunity may select (b), not realising the scenario's challenge is under Articles 14 and 19 (not Article 21 or basic structure), making Article 31C the precise answer.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a law implementing Article 39(b) challenged specifically under Articles 14 and 19 — the precise shield against such challenges is Article 31C.
Article 31C (post-Minerva Mills) protects laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 — this directly matches the challenge in the scenario.

Option (b) (Ninth Schedule): The Ninth Schedule provides immunity broadly from FR challenges under Article 31B — but the question asks specifically about the provision that enables the government to plead immunity against Articles 14 and 19 challenges on the law's face, which is Article 31C.
Option (c) (Article 38): Article 38 is a benchmark provision, not a shield against FR challenges.
Option (d) (Article 13): Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with FRs void — it is the provision being invoked against the government, not by it.
Confirm (a): Article 31C is the specific shield against Articles 14 and 19 challenges for 39(b)-implementing laws.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to test whether students know the difference between Article 31C (a targeted shield for 39(b) and 39(c) laws against Articles 14 and 19 specifically) and the Ninth Schedule (a broader immunity mechanism under Article 31B). Students who recall that 'Ninth Schedule provides immunity' will gravitate to option (b) without recognising that 31C is the more precise and primary legal basis for such a defence when the challenge is on Articles 14 and 19 grounds.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C (inserted by 25th Amendment, 1971, and limited to 39(b) and 39(c) after Minerva Mills) provides that laws enacted to implement Articles 39(b) and 39(c) shall not be deemed void on the ground that they are inconsistent with Articles 14 or 19.

Scenario: Parliament enacts a law redistributing ownership of certain industrial facilities to serve the common good (implementing Article 39(b)). The owners challenge it as violating their rights under Articles 14 (equality) and 19(1)(g) (freedom of trade). The government must identify the constitutional provision that most directly shields this law from such a challenge.

• Option (a) — Article 31C: Correct. This provision specifically immunises laws implementing 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 — the precise match for the scenario.
• Option (b) — Ninth Schedule: The Ninth Schedule provides broader immunity under Article 31B, but only for laws specifically placed in the Schedule. Article 31C is the more direct and precise shield applicable on the face of the legislation.
• Option (c) — Article 38: This is a directive on social order — not a shield against FR challenges.
• Option (d) — Article 13: Article 13 declares FR-inconsistent laws void — it is the petitioner's weapon, not the State's shield.

Value Addition:
• Post-Minerva Mills: 31C protection covers only 39(b) and 39(c) — not 41, 42, 43, or other DPSPs.
• Laws for 39(b) and 39(c) are immune from Articles 14 and 19 challenges — but NOT from Article 21 challenges.
• Kesavananda Bharati upheld 31C but struck down the clause barring judicial review — courts can still check whether the law genuinely implements 39(b)/(c).

solution.concept_anchor: FR-DPSP conflict evolution — Champakam to Minerva Mills to modern harmonisation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may place Kesavananda Bharati before Champakam Dorairajan if they associate 'the fundamental case' with Kesavananda's fame, not recalling that Champakam (1951) was the earlier foundational ruling.
elimination_logic: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) was the first major case — held FRs prevail over DPSPs. It came first.
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) upheld the original Article 31C but struck down the judicial review bar — it established basic structure and came second.
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down 42nd Amendment's extension of 31C to all DPSPs and established harmonisation as basic structure — it came third.
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) applied basic structure to Ninth Schedule laws post-1973 — the most recent of the four. Correct order: 1→2→3→4 = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who associate landmark constitutional cases by fame rather than chronology may place Kesavananda first (as the 'most important' case). Champakam Dorairajan (1951) is the first significant FR-DPSP conflict case but is overshadowed in general recall by the later landmark cases. The temporal-swap between 1951 and 1973 is the core trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The FR-DPSP relationship evolved through a series of Supreme Court rulings over six decades.

Correct sequence:
1. Champakam Dorairajan (1951): First major ruling — held Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles. Led directly to the First Amendment.
2. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Established the basic structure doctrine; upheld original Article 31C but struck down the judicial review bar within it.
3. Minerva Mills (1980): Struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of 31C to all DPSPs; established that harmonisation between FRs and DPSPs is basic structure.
4. I.R. Coelho (2007): Held that Ninth Schedule laws added after April 24, 1973 are subject to basic structure review — the final evolution in this jurisprudential sequence.

Wrong options: Options (a), (b), (c) misplace Champakam or reverse the order of Kesavananda and Minerva Mills.

Value Addition:
• Each ruling prompted constitutional amendment responses — Champakam → First Amendment; Kesavananda → 42nd Amendment attempt (partially); Coelho's doctrine remains judicially administered.
• Minerva Mills is the definitive case on FR-DPSP balance as basic structure.
• The basic structure doctrine was born in Kesavananda but applied to DPSP-FR relations in Minerva Mills.

solution.concept_anchor: Judicial enforcement route — 39(d) via Articles 14 and 16, unlike others
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 39(a) is linked to Article 21 (Olga Tellis) may think 39(a) is the odd one out because of this unusual judicial route, overlooking that 39(d) is uniquely enforced through Articles 14 and 16.
elimination_logic: The question groups DPSPs that are enforced primarily through their relationship with other constitutional provisions by courts.
Articles 39(a), 39(c), and 41 are all enforced in a similar general mode — used as interpretive aids or policy benchmarks, not elevated to FR status through a specific Articles 14/16 route.

Article 39(d) is uniquely distinguished: courts have specifically enforced it as a constitutional right by reading it with Articles 14 (equality) and 16 (equality in public employment) — a specific bi-provision enforcement route not used for the others.
Article 39(d)'s enforcement mechanism through Articles 14 and 16 specifically (Randhir Singh, 1982) distinguishes it — correct odd one out is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students may pick Article 39(a) because of the famous Olga Tellis linkage to Article 21. However, the distinguishing criterion here is the specific Articles 14 + 16 enforcement route — which belongs uniquely to Article 39(d). Articles 39(a), 39(c), and 41 are enforced as interpretive aids or policy benchmarks but do not have the specific bi-provision (14+16) judicial enforcement route that 39(d) acquired through Randhir Singh (1982). The entity-swap is between 39(a) and 39(d) as the 'odd' provision.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the specific judicial enforcement routes that courts have constructed for different socialist DPSPs.

• Option (a) — Article 39(a): Linked to Article 21 (right to life) through Olga Tellis — livelihood as part of life. Enforced through Article 21.
• Option (b) — Article 39(c): Used as a policy benchmark in competition law and monopoly regulation cases. No specific bi-provision judicial enforcement route.
• Option (c) — Article 39(d): The odd one out. In Randhir Singh (1982), the SC specifically enforced equal pay for equal work by reading Article 39(d) with Articles 14 (equality before law) AND 16 (equality in public employment) — a unique dual-provision enforcement route.
• Option (d) — Article 41: MGNREGA is a statutory realisation; courts use it as an interpretive aid but not through a specific Articles 14+16 route.

Value Addition:
• The Randhir Singh route (39(d) + 14 + 16) is the model for how DPSPs can acquire FR-like enforceability through judicial interpretation.
• Article 21's expanding scope (Maneka Gandhi, Francis Coralie) created the vehicle for 39(a)'s enforcement through Olga Tellis.
• The distinction between 'interpretive aid' and 'judicially enforceable right through specific FR articles' is the key analytical divide.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall the Maternity Benefit Act was amended during the UPA era may associate the extension with 2010 or 2012, not the 2017 NDA-era amendment.

The temporal-swap element is that students may attribute the amendment to an earlier year or a different government period, further muddying the recall of the specific figure.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 is the primary legislation implementing Article 42's maternity relief directive. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 significantly enhanced its provisions.

solution.concept_anchor: Correct classification — which DPSPs carry 'economic capacity' qualifier

statement_analysis.statement: Among the socialist DPSPs, Article 41 is the only provision that explicitly contains a qualifier limiting the State's obligation to its 'economic capacity and the stage of development'.
statement_analysis.reason: The 'within the limits of its economic capacity and development' qualifier appears uniquely in Article 41 — no other socialist DPSP contains such an explicit conditional limitation.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 43A requires the State to take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments, or other organisations engaged in any industry.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurate restatement of Article 43A's text — it covers undertakings, establishments, and other organisations engaged in any industry, without restricting to public sector alone.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 38 and Article 39(b) together constitute the 'equality code' of the Directive Principles, serving as the primary constitutional provisions specifically mandating equal distribution of political power among citizens.
statement_analysis.reason: This description is a fabrication. Article 38 is about social order and welfare; Article 39(b) is about material resource distribution. Neither specifically mandates 'equal distribution of political power' — that concept belongs to the Preamble and FR chapter, not to these two DPSP provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may accept Statement 3 because 'equality code' sounds plausible and the pairing of 38 with 39(b) seems logical, leading them to select 'all three'.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The economic-capacity qualifier is unique to Article 41 — no other socialist DPSP contains it. Mark correct.
Statement 2: Article 43A covers 'undertakings, establishments, or other organisations' engaged in any industry — this matches the provision's actual text. Mark correct.

Statement 3: The phrase 'equality code of Directive Principles' and 'equal distribution of political power' are not found in any standard constitutional interpretation — this is a plausible-fabrication pairing two real provisions with a false characterisation. Mark incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys the plausible-fabrication technique: it combines two real Articles (38 and 39(b)) with a convincing-sounding but entirely fictitious characterisation ('equality code' and 'equal distribution of political power'). Students who are unsure about the precise scope of Articles 38 and 39(b) may accept the authoritative-sounding description. The tell is the phrase 'political power' — Article 38 promotes social order and welfare; Article 39(b) is about material resources — neither deals with political power distribution.
solution.final_explanation:
The socialist DPSPs have specific constitutional functions that should not be conflated or fabricated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 41's 'within the limits of economic capacity and development' qualifier is unique among socialist DPSPs — it explicitly conditions the State's obligation, unlike Articles 39, 42, 43, 43A, or 43B.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 43A's mandate covers 'undertakings, establishments, or other organisations engaged in any industry' — broad language that extends beyond the public sector.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The description of Articles 38 and 39(b) as an 'equality code' mandating 'equal distribution of political power' is fabricated. Article 38 mandates a social welfare order; Article 39(b) is about material resource distribution. Neither uses the language of political power equality.

Value Addition:
• Article 41's economic-capacity qualifier has been cited in litigation to argue against judicial enforcement of 41's mandates as rights — a key distinction from Articles 39 sub-clauses.
• Article 43A's 'or in any other way' language gives Parliament flexibility in implementation mode.
• The Companies Act and Industrial Disputes Act are partial implementations of Article 43A — worker directors under company law are one expression.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31B of the Constitution provides that any Act or Regulation placed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be declared void on the ground that it takes away or abridges any Fundamental Right, without exception for any time period.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-I.R. Coelho (2007), this blanket immunity is qualified — laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) can be reviewed if they violate the basic structure. The 'without exception' claim is therefore incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The primary purpose for which the Ninth Schedule was created by the First Constitutional Amendment (1951) was to protect land reform and agrarian legislation implementing socialist Directive Principles from being struck down on Fundamental Rights grounds.
statement_analysis.reason: The First Amendment (1951) was a direct response to court rulings invalidating land reform laws. The Ninth Schedule was designed precisely to insulate such laws from FR challenges, implementing the socialist DPSP objectives on resource distribution.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who broadly recall that 'Ninth Schedule provides immunity' and 'was created for land reform' may accept both statements as correct without noticing the 'without exception' overstatement in Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 31B as read with the Ninth Schedule does provide immunity — but NOT without exception. After April 24, 1973 (I.R. Coelho ruling), laws added to the Schedule are subject to basic structure review. The 'without exception' phrase makes Statement 1 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The First Amendment (1951) created the Ninth Schedule specifically for land reform legislation — this is historically accurate and correctly stated. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — correct option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is carefully crafted with 'without exception' — which sounds like a constitutional absolute but is definitively qualified by the I.R. Coelho ruling. Students who recall Article 31B's blanket immunity principle without remembering the post-Coelho qualification will mark Statement 1 as correct. The partial-truth trap: 31B does provide immunity, but not without exception — the temporal limitation from Coelho is the critical qualifier.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule and Article 31B form a protective shield for land reform and socialist legislation.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 31B does provide that Ninth Schedule laws cannot be declared void for abridging FRs, but the I.R. Coelho ruling (2007) created an important exception — laws added after April 24, 1973 (the Kesavananda date) are subject to judicial review for violations of basic structure. The 'without exception' claim is therefore incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The First Amendment (1951) added Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule in direct response to judicial invalidation of land reform laws. Protecting the implementation of socialist DPSPs on resource distribution was its explicit purpose.

Value Addition:
• The Ninth Schedule currently contains over 280 laws — primarily land reform, minority educational institution regulations, and other welfare legislation.
• Pre-1973 Ninth Schedule laws enjoy complete immunity; post-1973 laws are subject to basic structure scrutiny.
• The Kesavananda date (April 24, 1973) is the constitutionally significant dividing line across multiple areas of constitutional law.
